analysis.one_liner: Let consumers tell online companies not to collect their personal data, with FTC and state enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee in February 2013 and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Trade Commission to set up a simple 'do-not-track' mechanism, similar to the do-not-call list, letting people tell online service providers and mobile apps not to collect their personal information. Companies that ignored that preference could be fined or sued, with enforcement shared between the FTC and state attorneys general. The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday internet and mobile users, who would gain a simple, enforceable way to stop companies from tracking what they do online and on their phones.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC to set standards for a simple mechanism letting individuals indicate they prefer not to have personal information collected by online service providers, including mobile apps.

Prohibits providers from collecting personal information from people who expressed that preference, except for information needed to deliver a requested service (with anonymization or deletion) or where the person got clear notice and gave affirmative consent.

Enforces the rules through the FTC and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for injunctions, damages, restitution, and civil penalties, with penalties that rise with the number of days out of compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Online service providers, including social media platforms, mobile app developers, and the advertising industry built on tracking people's activity across sites and apps, which would lose much of the behavioral data used to target ads and shape services.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the FTC to weigh the technical feasibility and costs of compliance, acknowledging that implementing and honoring tracking preferences carries real costs for online businesses, which could be passed to consumers or affect free services supported by targeted advertising.

The bill carries a potential hidden cost for consumers: services funded by behaviorally targeted advertising could respond by charging fees, showing more intrusive non-tracked ads, or degrading free offerings, since ad revenue depends on tracking.

The bill does not directly give individuals a private right of action; enforcement rests with the FTC and state AGs, so an individual who believes they were tracked in violation of the rules would have to rely on agencies to act.

The bill allows continued collection with notice and affirmative consent, meaning companies could still track anyone who clicks through a consent screen, and the FTC's scope decisions could limit how much tracking is actually covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: real control over whether companies can compile a record of what they do online and on their phones, backed by penalties. The main cost is to the ad-tech industry, whose business model depends on that data. Legitimate concerns exist that free, ad-supported services could get worse or start charging, and that consent exceptions could blunt the rules, but the bill's core offer — an enforceable opt-out of behavioral tracking — is the kind of protection the do-not-call list provided for phones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on February 28, 2013, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator John D. Rockefeller IV on February 28, 2013, with Senator Richard Blumenthal as a cosponsor, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action appears in the full action history — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, at which point the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The online advertising and data-tracking industry is better off: because the bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, companies were never required to honor a do-not-track preference or face FTC and state enforcement, and they kept the behavioral data their ad businesses run on. Internet users, who would have gained the opt-out, are left no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-WV); bill sponsor; Chairman, Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do-Not-Track Online Act of 2013 on February 28, 2013.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral on February 28, 2013; the bill sat without action until Congress ended.

against.name: Online advertising and data-tracking industry
against.role: Industry with a business model dependent on behavioral tracking
against.what_they_did: The bill's passage would have cost this industry its core data; the record does not show their activity, but the bill dying without a hearing left their data practices untouched.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats in a Senate controlled by Democrats, and with only one cosponsor and no recorded floor action, the bill never got far enough for a partisan roll call to reveal how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Online advertising and behavioral data brokers
industries.note: The bill would have barred companies from collecting personal information from people who opted out of tracking, cutting off the behavioral data used to target ads and price data-driven services. Industry interests run against the public's interest in controlling their own data, which is why the bill's death without a hearing left the industry's data practices fully intact.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and mobile app providers
industries.note: These companies both gather data used for ads and provide the services people use; the bill would have restricted data collection but allowed continued collection for basic service functionality or with consent, so the hit to their data pipelines would have been real but not absolute.

The bill would have expanded the FTC's authority to police tracking practices and given state attorneys general a new civil enforcement tool with damages and per-day civil penalties, strengthening their ability to act on behalf of consumers.
